strong.name: Strong
strong.definition: Meta-analyses of classroom studies show that working this way improves learning.

promising.name: Promising
promising.definition: Controlled studies show gains, but results are mixed, small in number or dependent on context.

framework.name: Framework
framework.definition: A useful structure. The method itself has not been tested in intervention studies.

choosewise.name: Choosewise
choosewise.definition: Our own rule, not a research finding.

lines.job: Says who the message is for.

lines.text: [First name] explained [idea] clearly in class this week.
One question to ask at home: [question, for example 'Can you explain this without your book?']
lines.job: One thing to do at home.

sections.title: Meetings about teaching
sections.intro: Give each meeting about teaching one problem in your teaching, and end it with a decision that each of you tries in class. Send information in writing instead, and keep the meeting for teaching.

templates.title: Meeting protocol
templates.intro: One problem per meeting, a decision that each of you tries in class, and a follow-up at the next meeting.

blocks.heading: The problem
lines: One problem many of us see in class, in one sentence.

blocks.heading: What each of us brings
lines: A task, a test item or a count from an exit ticket. Student work stays on paper in the room, with names removed, and never goes into an AI tool.

blocks.heading: What we saw
lines: What the things we brought show about the problem.

blocks.heading: The decision
lines: The one change each of us tries in class.

blocks.heading: Who, by when
lines: Each of us, and the date we try the change by.

blocks.heading: Follow-up
lines: Date: [date of the next meeting]
What we will look at: [what we will bring to check the change]
What happened (filled in at the next meeting):

blocks.heading: Decision log
lines: Date | Decision | Result

templates.title: Information note
templates.intro: Send this instead of a meeting that only passes on information. Keep the meeting for teaching.

blocks.heading: Who it is for
lines: [team or group]

blocks.heading: What is new
lines: [what has changed, in one or two sentences]

blocks.heading: What you need to do, by when
lines: [what to do] by [date]

blocks.heading: Who to ask
lines: [name], [how to reach them]

blocks.heading: For the next meeting
lines: Questions we will take at [meeting]: [only what needs discussion]

templates.title: Skill pairing
templates.intro: Pair up with the colleague who is strong at exactly the skill you want to get better at. The visits and the fifteen-minute talk are our rule, not a research finding.

blocks.heading: One skill to get better at
lines: [the skill, for example starting a lesson, explaining a hard idea or giving feedback]

blocks.heading: The colleague
lines: [colleague's name], who is strong at exactly this skill

blocks.heading: One visit each way
lines: I watch one of [colleague's name]'s lessons on [date].
[Colleague's name] watches one of mine on [date].

blocks.heading: Fifteen minutes' talk afterwards
lines: What I saw:
What I will try:
When we check: [date]

prompts.title: An agenda for a meeting about one problem
prompts.body: Our team of [number] teachers of [subject or year group] has [length] minutes to work on one problem in our teaching: [the problem]. Write an agenda with times: what each of us brings (a task, a test item or a count from an exit ticket), how we look at it together, the one change we will each try in class, and when and how we check the result at the next meeting. Do not ask me about individual students or colleagues.

prompts.title: An information note instead of a meeting
prompts.body: I want to send my team a written note instead of holding a meeting that only passes on information. Here are the points: [list the points]. Turn them into a note under 200 words in plain language, with four parts: who it is for, what is new, what they need to do and by when, and who to ask. If a point needs discussion, do not explain it in the note; list it at the end as a question for our next meeting. Do not ask me for names or details about students or colleagues.

sections.title: Administration
sections.intro: Cut first, then standardise what is left. Go through your team's recurring documents, stop what nobody acts on, and turn the rest into one-page templates with placeholders.

templates.title: Cut first checklist
templates.intro: Go through your team's recurring documents together. Ask three questions of each, then keep, shorten or stop it.

blocks.heading: Our recurring documents
lines: Document | Who reads it | What do they do with it | What would happen without it | Keep, shorten or stop

blocks.heading: Five checks, with examples from England
lines: No more than two or three data collections a year, each used for a clear action (DfE 2018).
No marking done to leave a trail (DfE 2016).
Short reports instead of long written ones (DfE 2018).
One-page policies that leave the method to teachers (EEF feedback guidance, 2021).
"If the hours spent do not have the commensurate impact on pupil progress: stop it." (DfE 2016)
The DfE (England's Department for Education) and the EEF (Education Endowment Foundation) are examples from England. Check what applies where you work.

templates.title: One-page letter template
templates.intro: For a letter you write again and again: a trip, a test date, an event. Everything personal stays in brackets until you fill it in, outside AI.

blocks.heading: Who it is for and what they need to do
lines: To the parents and guardians of [class or year group]: please [what they need to do] by [date].

blocks.heading: What, when, where
lines: What: [the trip, test or event]
When: [date and time]
Where: [place]

blocks.heading: What to bring or decide
lines: [what to bring, or what to decide]

blocks.heading: Reply
lines: Please reply by [date] to [name], [how to reply].
[Your name], [school]

prompts.title: A one-page template for a recurring document
prompts.body: I am a teacher at a [primary or secondary] school. Write a one-page template for a document I write again and again: [the document, for example a letter to parents about a trip]. Put every name, date, grade and personal detail in square brackets as a placeholder. Start with one line saying who it is for and what they need to do. Keep it short and plain. Do not ask me for names or details about students.

prompts.title: A policy or routine on one page
prompts.body: Here is our school's own text for a policy or routine: [paste the text, with no names or personal details]. Shorten it to one page. Keep what someone has to act on: who does what, and by when. Leave the method and how often to do it to the teachers. Then list everything you removed, so our team can check it. Do not ask me for names or details about students or colleagues.

sections.country_line: Rules differ between countries. Check what applies where you work before you stop keeping a record or change what you document.

sections.title: Messages home
sections.intro: Short, regular messages about one specific thing: work that is missing, a test that is coming, something done well. Agree with your team how many messages a class gets per term, and stay within that limit.

templates.title: Messages home
templates.intro: Four messages, each under 60 words, and a plan for the term. Fill in the brackets one message at a time, outside AI, and read each message before you send it.

blocks.heading: Missing work
lines: Hello [parent's name]. [First name] has [number] pieces of work missing in [subject]: [the work]. Please help [first name] hand them in by [date]. One question to ask at home: [question, for example 'Which one will you finish first?']
[Your name]

blocks.heading: An upcoming test
lines: Hello [parent's name]. [First name]'s class has a test on [topic] on [date]. It covers [what the test covers]. A tip for revising: [one revision tip]. One question to ask at home: [question, for example 'Can you explain this without your book?']
[Your name]

blocks.heading: Something done well
lines: Hello [parent's name]. [First name] [something specific done well] in [subject] this week. One thing to work on next: [one thing]. One question to ask at home: [question]
[Your name]

blocks.heading: Absence
lines: Hello [parent's name]. So far this term, [first name] has been absent for [number] days in total. Every day in school helps [first name] keep up with the class. Is there anything we can do to help?
[Your name]

blocks.heading: Term plan
lines: Messages per class this term, as agreed with our team: [number]
Date | Class | Template
Keep student names out of this log.

prompts.title: Three message templates
prompts.body: I teach [subject] to [age or year group]. Write three message templates to parents or guardians, each under 60 words and in plain language: one about missing work, one about an upcoming test, and one about something done well with one thing to work on. Use square brackets for every name, date, number and detail, for example [first name], [date] and [topic]. End each message with one question the family can ask at home. Do not ask me about individual students.

prompts.title: Translate a template
prompts.body: Translate this message template into [language]: [paste the template]. Keep every square bracket and its contents unchanged, in English, so that I can fill them in afterwards. Use plain, everyday words. After the translation, list any phrase that may not carry over well into [language], and suggest another way to say it. Do not ask me for names or details about students, their families or colleagues.

prompts.title: Rewrite a template in plain language
prompts.body: Rewrite this message template in plain language: [paste the template]. Write so that a parent with little schooling, or someone still learning the language, can understand it. Use short sentences and everyday words. Keep the same facts and the same request. Keep every square bracket and its contents unchanged. Do not ask me for names or details about students, their families or colleagues.

sections.country_line: Rules differ between countries. Check what applies where you work before you send messages home, store parents' contact details or translate for families.

evidence.title: Meetings about one problem, quality over hours
evidence.label: promising
evidence.text: In a study of more than 9,000 teachers in 336 Miami-Dade schools, it was better quality of collaboration that went with larger gains in maths and reading (Ronfeldt et al. 2015). It is a correlation, not a measured cause. The meeting protocol itself is a Framework: we have found no trial of a meeting protocol on its own.

sources.text: Ronfeldt, Farmer, McQueen & Grissom 2015, American Educational Research Journal

evidence.title: Pairing on a skill
evidence.label: promising
evidence.text: In a randomised trial, pairing teachers who scored low on specific skills with colleagues strong in those skills raised student achievement in the low-scoring teachers' classes by 0.12 standard deviations, a small effect (Papay et al. 2020). That is smaller than coaching (0.18 on achievement across 60 causal studies; Kraft et al. 2018), but it came from a colleague rather than a programme. It is a single trial.

sources.text: Papay, Taylor, Tyler & Laski 2020, American Economic Journal: Economic Policy
Kraft, Blazar & Hogan 2018, Review of Educational Research

evidence.title: Content matters more than format
evidence.text: The EEF's trial of lesson study in 181 English primary schools found that pupils did no better on national tests a year after the two-year programme (Murphy et al. 2021). A US trial with 39 teams found larger gains in fractions knowledge when lesson study came with a research-based resource kit (Lewis & Perry 2017). Our reading: what the team brings to look at matters more than the format of the meeting.

sources.text: Murphy, Weinhardt & Wyness 2021, Economics of Education Review
Lewis & Perry 2017, Journal for Research in Mathematics Education

evidence.title: Cut first
evidence.label: framework
evidence.text: England's Department for Education saw "no reason" for more than two or three attainment data collection points a year, each used to inform clear actions, and called lengthy written reports to parents "usually burdensome" (DfE 2018). Its marking review lists deep marking and writing "VF" to show that verbal feedback was given as ineffective practice, and says: "If the hours spent do not have the commensurate impact on pupil progress: stop it." (DfE 2016). The EEF's feedback guidance says a policy "should not over-specify features such as the frequency or method of feedback" (EEF 2021). These are examples from England. The guidance comes from expert groups, not from trials, and its value lies in cutting tasks, not in automating them.

sources.text: Department for Education 2018, Making data work (Teacher Workload Advisory Group)
Department for Education 2016, Eliminating unnecessary workload around marking
Education Endowment Foundation 2021, Teacher Feedback to Improve Pupil Learning

evidence.title: Messages about learning
evidence.label: promising
evidence.text: In US middle and high schools, weekly automated alerts about missed assignments, grades and absences cut course failures by 27% and raised class attendance by 12%, but did not change state test scores (Bergman & Chan 2021). In a high-school credit-recovery programme, a weekly one-sentence message from the teacher cut the share who failed to earn credit from 15.8% to 9.3% (Kraft & Rogers 2015). In a UK trial, 30 texts over a year about tests, homework and topics gave secondary students about one month's extra progress in maths, a small gain (via the EEF's guidance). The EEF says there is, as yet, less rigorous evidence for what makes parental engagement effective, and that many of the more rigorous studies show mixed results; the impacts of well-designed messages may appear small, but they are generally low cost.

sources.text: Bergman & Chan 2021, Journal of Human Resources
Kraft & Rogers 2015, Economics of Education Review
Education Endowment Foundation 2018, Working with Parents to Support Children's Learning

evidence.title: Short absence letters
evidence.label: promising
evidence.text: In 203 US schools, a letter with the child's total days absent, in fewer than 50 words and without blame, cut absences by about one day per child (Rogers & Feller 2018, as reported in the EEF's guidance). The absence message in this pack follows that pattern.

sources.text: Education Endowment Foundation 2018, Working with Parents to Support Children's Learning

evidence.title: AI for these tasks
evidence.text: We have found no controlled study of AI for report writing or parent communication. Checking is work too: interviews with 57 teachers in Sweden and Australia, reported by the OECD, describe the hidden labour of reviewing and repairing AI drafts for administrative tasks (Selwyn, Ljungqvist & Sonesson 2025). That is why AI writes the template here, and you add the details afterwards, outside AI.

sources.text: Selwyn, Ljungqvist & Sonesson 2025, Learning, Media and Technology

care.risk: Wrong details in the wrong message.
care.what_we_do: Fill in the brackets one message at a time, outside AI, and read each message before you send it.
Keep every template to one page. If a template gets longer than what it replaced, cut it.
Count what already goes out to each class, and stay within the limit your team agreed.
Translate the template before any details go in, keep the brackets unchanged, and where you can, ask someone who reads the language to check it once.
Give each meeting one problem, and spread the rest over later meetings.
